questions.text_verbatim: Reducing the speed of main propulsion engines is considered to be the simplest and most practical short-term solution for lowering GHG emissions from ships. blocks.h: 1. Why speed reduction is attractive, and what "low load" costs

blocks.p: Propulsion power varies roughly with the cube of ship speed, so a modest speed reduction gives a large fuel and CO2 saving at no capital cost - which is why MARPOL Annex VI regulation 25 (EEXI) and regulation 28 (CII), in force since 1 January 2023, are often met by slowing down. The cost is that a two-stroke is optimised around roughly 70-80% MCR, and running far below that puts every balance - air to fuel, thermal and lubrication - outside its design condition.

ul: Reduced scavenge air pressure. The turbocharger is sized for high load, so at low load the air-fuel ratio falls and combustion is incomplete.
Low compression and maximum pressure, giving late, slow burning and poor thermal efficiency.
Poorer atomisation where injection pressure depends on speed - large droplets, afterburning, and cool nozzles prone to dribbling and trumpet deposits.
Soot and unburnt fuel through the whole gas path - piston crown, exhaust valve, receiver, turbine nozzle ring and economiser.
Surging, from running close to the compressor surge line and aggravated by a fouled turbine side, with mechanical damage to rotor and bearings.
Auxiliary blowers running continuously, because scavenge pressure never rises enough to cut them out.
Scavenge space and port fouling by oil-soaked carbon - the classic precondition for a scavenge fire.
Fouled nozzle rings and blades, reducing air supply further: a self-reinforcing loop.

blocks.h: 4. Cylinder condition - cold corrosion and lubrication

blocks.p: This is the most damaging effect. Lower heat release lets the liner wall fall below the acid dew point, so sulphuric acid formed from fuel sulphur and water vapour condenses on it. The result is cold corrosion - rapid corrosive wear concentrated near the top ring reversal point. It is aggravated when cylinder oil BN is not matched to the duty, or when feed rate is cut for economy; the opposite error, persistent over-lubrication, gives deposits, bore polishing and eventually scuffing. Low-sulphur fuel does not remove the problem - it changes the correct oil BN.

ul: Exhaust gas economiser. Low exhaust temperature and flow cut steam production, so the auxiliary boiler must run - eroding the saving - while soot builds on the tubes. A later load increase can ignite it as a soot fire.
Exhaust valves running cool, with deposits, poor rotation and seat blow-by.
Manoeuvring: reduced propeller inflow gives less rudder authority, and prolonged running near a barred speed range must be avoided.
Hull and propeller fouling increases at low speed and during warm-water idling, degrading the very efficiency sought.

blocks.h: 6. Engineering measures to resolve the problems

ul: Low-load or part-load tuning, so injection and exhaust valve timing suit the new band. On electronically controlled engines this is a control change, not mechanical rework.
Turbocharger cut-out on multi-turbocharger engines, or variable turbine area or an exhaust bypass, to restore scavenge pressure and move away from surge.
Cylinder lubrication set from evidence: match BN to fuel sulphur and liner condition, and set feed rate from scavenge drain analysis (iron content, residual BN) and scrape-down inspection.
Raise liner wall temperature where the design allows, by jacket water control or liner insulation, to keep the surface above the acid dew point.
Where slowing down is used for EEXI compliance, implement it as an approved engine or shaft power limitation with a sealed, recorded override, documented in the technical file and accepted by class.
Planned periodic load-up runs to burn off deposits, taken in the passage rather than left to a manoeuvring situation.
More frequent scavenge space inspection and economiser soot blowing and water washing, treating the boiler as a fire risk before any load increase.
Condition monitoring - PMI pressure analysis, exhaust deviation, turbocharger speed against scavenge pressure, and liner wear at shorter intervals than the maker's baseline.
Update the SEEMP and the maintenance plan to the new profile: the engine is running in a condition those intervals were not written for.

blocks.p: Speed reduction is the cheapest short-term carbon measure, but not a free one: it moves the engine outside its design envelope and transfers cost from fuel to wear, fouling and fire risk. Retuned, correctly lubricated and monitored, those risks are controllable; unmanaged, cold corrosion and scavenge or economiser fires are the predictable results.

The question has two explicit halves - drawbacks and dangers, then how they are resolved. A common failure is to write a long list of problems and then two lines of remedies. Give the second half real weight: roughly nine or ten marks of problems and six or seven of solutions. Grouping the problems by where they occur (combustion, turbocharger and scavenge, cylinder, everything else) rather than as an undifferentiated list also shows you understand the mechanism rather than having memorised a list.

blocks.h: The central mechanism - get this right and the rest follows

blocks.p: Almost every drawback traces back to one fact: the turbocharger is sized for high load and cannot deliver design air at low load. Less air gives incomplete combustion; incomplete combustion gives soot; soot fouls the turbine and economiser; a fouled turbine gives still less air. Separately, less heat release lowers liner wall temperature, and below the acid dew point that produces cold corrosion. If you can state those two chains, you can derive the whole answer in the exam without recalling a list.

ul: Treating cold corrosion as a low-sulphur-fuel problem. It is a liner temperature problem. Low-sulphur fuel changes the correct cylinder oil BN; it does not remove condensation.
Claiming a specific percentage of MCR as the universal definition of 'low load'. The band depends on engine type and tuning - say 'well below the design point of roughly 70-80% MCR' instead.
Forgetting the exhaust gas economiser entirely. It is where a low-load soot fire actually starts, and it is worth marks.
Answering only about the main engine when the question says 'risks associated with low speed operation' - manoeuvrability, hull fouling and auxiliary boiler load are part of the picture.
Presenting engine power limitation as something a Chief Engineer simply sets. It is an approved arrangement recorded in the EEXI technical file, with a controlled override.

blocks.p:
"So slow steaming saves fuel - what is the problem?" The trap is to agree too readily. The correct engineering answer is that the fuel saving is real but partly offset by auxiliary boiler firing, increased maintenance and hull fouling, and it carries fire and wear risks that must be actively managed.

"Which regulation makes you slow down?" None does. EEXI (regulation 25) is a technical index and CII (regulation 28) is an operational rating; speed reduction is a common means of compliance, not a requirement. Saying "MARPOL requires slow steaming" is wrong.

blocks.h: Currency - what was true in January 2026

blocks.p: At the date of this paper, EEXI and CII were in force and had been since 1 January 2023. The IMO Net-Zero Framework was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 but its adoption was adjourned at the extraordinary MEPC session of 14 to 17 October 2025, to reconvene twelve months later. So in January 2026 - and still as at August 2026 - the Net-Zero Framework was not adopted and not in force. Do not write that a global GHG fuel standard or carbon price is in force. If you mention the Framework, say it is approved and awaiting adoption.

ul: Why does cold corrosion concentrate at the top of the liner? That is where the wall is coolest relative to the gas and where the top ring reverses, so condensed acid is mechanically worked into the surface.
How would you know cold corrosion is happening before you open up? Rising iron content in scavenge drain oil analysis with falling residual BN, and accelerating liner wear measurements.
Why must you be careful increasing load after a long slow-steaming passage? Accumulated soot in the economiser can ignite. Soot blow first, and raise load in stages.
What is turbocharger cut-out and when is it used? Isolating one turbocharger on a multi-turbocharger engine at low load to restore scavenge pressure and move away from surge.

Does low-sulphur fuel mean you can use a low-BN cylinder oil? It means you should match BN to sulphur - but if the liner is running cold you may still need alkalinity, so decide on drain analysis, not on fuel grade alone.

blocks.p: Work outward from the cylinder: AIR - BURN - WALL - REST. Air: turbocharger cannot supply design air (steps 2 and 3). Burn: incomplete combustion, soot, fouling. Wall: liner too cold, cold corrosion, lubrication mismatch (step 4). Rest: economiser, exhaust valves, manoeuvring, hull (step 5). Then the two remedy steps are simply fix the machine (step 6) and fix the operation (step 7).

ul: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 25 - Attained EEXI, required for existing ships; engine or shaft power limitation is an accepted means of achieving it
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 26 - SEEMP, with Part III for the CII plan
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28 - operational carbon intensity indicator and A to E rating
IMO Net-Zero Framework - approved MEPC 83 (April 2025); adoption ADJOURNED at the extraordinary MEPC session, 14 to 17 October 2025, to reconvene twelve months later; not adopted, not in force
Engine-designer service guidance on part-load / low-load tuning, turbocharger cut-out and cylinder oil feed rate - industry guidance, not regulation
SOLAS II-1 and class requirements for scavenge and economiser fire precautions - the safety context for the fire risks described

blocks.p: The regulatory statements in this answer are verified against IMO primary sources. The engineering content is established marine-engineering principle supported by engine-designer service guidance, and it is written to apply generally to large slow-speed two-stroke engines. It is deliberately not tied to one designer's figures: load thresholds, tuning options, permissible jacket water temperatures and cylinder oil recommendations differ between engine types and between tuning packages, and the ship's own maker documentation and class approval govern in every case. Where this answer says 'roughly 70-80% MCR' it is describing the usual optimisation region, not a specification. Whether a specific ship may apply engine power limitation, and on what conditions, depends on its own EEXI technical file and class acceptance.

questions.understand_first: A large two-stroke engine and its turbocharger are matched to each other at one region of load, usually somewhere around three-quarters power. Slow steaming does not simply make the engine do less of the same thing - it moves the engine to a place the matching was never designed for. Too little air for the fuel, and too little heat to keep the liner above the temperature at which acid condenses on it. Almost every drawback in this question is one of those two facts working its way outward.
questions.memory_cue: AIR (2, 3), WALL (4), REST (5), then fix the machine (6) and fix the operation (7).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What causes cold corrosion, and where does it appear?
retrieval_cards.answer: Reduced heat release lets the liner wall fall below the acid dew point, so sulphuric acid formed from fuel sulphur and water vapour condenses on it. The wear concentrates near the top piston-ring reversal point.
retrieval_cards.why: It is a liner temperature problem, not simply a fuel sulphur problem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does low-sulphur fuel remove the cold corrosion risk?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It changes the cylinder oil BN that is appropriate. Condensation still occurs if the liner runs below the acid dew point, so feed rate and BN should be set from scavenge drain analysis and liner wear, not from fuel grade alone.
retrieval_cards.why: A very common and confidently made error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does MARPOL require ships to slow steam?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. EEXI (Annex VI reg 25) is a technical index and CII (reg 28) is an operational rating. Speed reduction is a common means of complying with them, not a requirement in itself.
retrieval_cards.why: Examiners test whether you can separate a requirement from a means of compliance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What was the status of the IMO Net-Zero Framework in January 2026?
retrieval_cards.answer: Approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, but adoption was adjourned at the extraordinary MEPC session of 14 to 17 October 2025 for twelve months. It was therefore not adopted and not in force.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating it as in force is a currency error that dates an answer instantly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is increasing load after a long slow-steaming passage a fire risk, and what do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Soot accumulated in the exhaust gas economiser can ignite. Soot blow and, if required, water wash before load-up, then raise load in stages while monitoring exhaust and boiler temperatures.
retrieval_cards.why: A soot fire can escalate to an iron fire if the water side dries out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name four engineering measures that restore air supply or reduce low-load penalties.
retrieval_cards.answer: Low-load or part-load tuning of injection and exhaust valve timing; turbocharger cut-out on multi-turbocharger engines; variable turbine area or exhaust bypass; raising liner wall temperature by jacket water control or liner insulation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Roughly where is a large two-stroke optimised, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Around 70-80% MCR, approximately and depending on engine type and tuning. Sustained running well below that band is what puts the air, thermal and lubrication balances outside their design condition.
retrieval_cards.why: Give it as an approximate band - a single universal figure would be wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish EPL/ShaPoLi from simply ordering a slower speed.
retrieval_cards.answer: Engine or shaft power limitation is an approved arrangement recorded in the ship's EEXI technical file and accepted by class, with a sealed and recorded override available for safety. Ordering a slower speed is an operational decision with no such status.
retrieval_cards.why: Only the approved arrangement counts towards attained EEXI.

blocks.p: Communication is the transfer of information, instructions and meaning from a sender to a receiver through a channel, understood by the receiver as the sender intended. It is complete not when the message is sent but when feedback confirms it was understood. That feedback loop is what distinguishes communication from broadcasting.

ul: Verbal - face to face, telephone, UHF/VHF, public address: fast, immediate feedback, no record.
Written - work orders, permits, risk assessments, checklists, night orders, log books, handovers: slower but auditable, and what the safety management system relies on.
Non-verbal - hand signals, body language, and the visual and audible alarm system. In high noise this becomes the primary channel.
Formal and informal - the first recorded and following the organisational chart; the second quicker but unverified.
Vertical and horizontal - downward orders, upward reports and concerns, lateral between departments. Upward communication fails first, and safety depends on it.
Internal and external, and electronic - ship to shore, port, VTS and class; email, planned maintenance systems and alarm data.
Physical - engine room noise, distance, hearing protection, radio dead spots, intervening structure.
Language and semantic - multinational crews, differing fluency, jargon. Addressed by the working language required under SOLAS V/14.3 and ISM element 6.
Hierarchical and cultural - reluctance to question a senior. This is the barrier most often behind an accident everybody could see coming.
Physiological - fatigue, hearing loss, stress, time pressure, complacency on a routine job.
Organisational - unclear responsibility, two people each believing the other is in charge, poor handover.
Assumption - believing a message was understood because nobody asked. Silence is not confirmation.

blocks.h: 4. Where communication failure becomes a hazard in this job

blocks.p: The defining feature is vertical separation with a shared machine between the two groups: each can alter the condition of the engine the other is working inside, and neither can see the other. Hence:

ul: Turning gear operated with a person in the crankcase or under a piston - the most serious risk in the job.
Starting air admitted, or the main starting air valve left un-isolated, with the engine opened up.
Dropped objects - tools, nuts or debris falling from the cylinder head platform onto the group below.
Uncoordinated lifting of a piston, liner or head through the space while men work beneath the load path.
Hydraulic tensioning tools pressurised while another person handles the studs or nuts.
Systems restored by a third party - a standby pump starting on auto, or the control room restoring a system, releasing hot oil or water onto open work.
Enclosed space entry to crankcase or scavenge space without the other group knowing anyone is inside.
Shift handover - the incoming group not knowing what is isolated, what is slack, and where people are.

blocks.h: 5. Risk mitigation - organise the job before it starts

ul: A risk assessment and permit to work, with a separate enclosed space entry permit for crankcase or scavenge space.
One named person in overall charge and one leader per group. Nobody moves the engine except on that person's order.
A joint toolbox talk before starting: sequence, who is where, isolations, communication plan and the stop-work rule.
Lock-out and tag-out of turning gear supply, starting air, hydraulic power pack and standby pumps, tagged at the control room and at every local starter, with the key held by the person in charge.

blocks.h: 6. Risk mitigation - the communication plan itself

ul: A dedicated radio channel for the job, with headsets compatible with hearing protection, tested before work begins.
Closed-loop communication as the standing rule - instruction given, repeated back, execution confirmed. Turning the engine is announced, acknowledged by both groups, and only then carried out.
Agreed standard phrases and a hand-signal set for when radios fail or noise defeats them.
Confirm understanding by asking a person to state back what they are about to do - never by asking "do you understand?"
An explicit stop-work authority for everyone, stated at the toolbox talk so that using it is expected rather than brave.

blocks.h: 7. Risk mitigation - physical and record controls

ul: Avoid work directly above and below where the sequence allows; otherwise an exclusion zone, gratings or covers, and tethered tools.
A written handover at each shift change and a job log of isolations, work done and personnel inside the engine.
A personnel tally for crankcase and scavenge space entry, checked before any isolation is removed.
Formal permit close-out, confirming all persons and tools clear before turning gear is disengaged and the engine restored.

blocks.p: Here the machine is the message path: what one group does is felt immediately by the other. The controls that matter are specific, not exhortations - one person in charge, isolation that a misunderstanding cannot undo, closed-loop confirmation before the engine moves, and a written handover. Communication failure in this job does not cause inconvenience; it causes fatalities.

This is four questions in one, and the marks follow the work. The first three limbs are standard theory that every candidate can write, so they do not discriminate - keep them tight and complete. The scenario limb is where the marks are actually won, because it requires you to apply the theory to a specific engineering operation. Give roughly half the answer to limbs 4 to 7. A candidate who writes three pages on types and barriers and then two generic lines about 'good communication' has answered the easy part of the question and missed the point of it.

blocks.h: The word decarbonisation means the overhaul, not GHG

blocks.p: Read the scenario carefully. In this question "Main engine decarbonisation" means the traditional overhaul job - removing carbon deposits, pistons, liners, exhaust valves and heads - with men on the cylinder head platform above and on the bottom platform below. It does not mean greenhouse gas decarbonisation, even though Q1 of the same paper is about GHG reduction. Writing about carbon intensity here would lose the entire second half of the question. The tell is the physical description of two working platforms.

blocks.h: The organising idea for the scenario limb

blocks.p: One sentence carries the whole limb: two groups, vertically separated, working on one machine that either of them can move or pressurise. Every hazard is a consequence - what falls from above, what moves in between, and what a third party can restore from the control room. If you state that principle first and then derive the hazards, the list writes itself and reads as analysis rather than recall.

ul: Misreading 'decarbonisation' as GHG reduction and losing the scenario limb entirely.
Listing barriers without saying which ones bite in an engine room. Noise, hearing protection and radio dead spots are the specific ones; hierarchy is the dangerous one.

Giving mitigations that are slogans - 'improve communication', 'hold meetings'. Marks come from named controls: permit to work, lock-out/tag-out, closed-loop confirmation, exclusion zone, written handover.
Forgetting the third party. Many real accidents come from the engine control room or another watch restoring a system, not from either working group.
Defining communication without feedback. A definition that stops at 'transfer of information' misses the element every subsequent barrier attacks.

blocks.p:
"You briefed them - so you communicated, didn't you?" No. A briefing is transmission. Communication is complete only when understanding is confirmed, which is why the answer asks people to state back what they are about to do rather than asking whether they understood.

"Who may stop this job?" The expected answer is anyone. If you say only the Chief Engineer or the person in charge may stop it, you have described the hierarchical barrier you just finished criticising.

"Which single control would you keep if you could keep only one?" Physical isolation with lock-out and tag-out. Procedures depend on people communicating correctly; isolation survives a communication failure, which is exactly what is being guarded against.

ul: What is closed-loop communication? Instruction given, repeated back by the receiver, execution confirmed - so a misheard order is caught before it is acted on.

What must be isolated before crankcase entry on this job? Turning gear power supply, starting air, hydraulic power pack and standby lubricating oil and cooling water pumps, locked and tagged, with the key controlled.
Where is the working language requirement? SOLAS regulation V/14.3, supported by ISM Code element 6 on resources and personnel.
Why is upward communication the critical one? Because defects, doubts and refusals to proceed travel upward, and hierarchy suppresses them.
What do you record at handover? Isolations in place, work completed and in progress, tools and personnel inside the engine, and any change to the plan.

The application: Hazards (step 4), then three families of control - Organise the job (step 5), Communication plan (step 6), Physical and paper controls (step 7). Within the hazards, work top to bottom: what falls, what turns, what is pressurised, who else can restore a system.

The list of hazards is not claimed to be exhaustive - a real job requires its own risk assessment with the people who will do it. Where this answer names a control, it is describing what a competent management-level engineer should expect to see, not asserting that any particular convention mandates that specific control.

blocks.p: Modern salvage law rests on the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, in force since 14 July 1996, which replaced a purely property-based regime with one that also rewards protection of the environment. Its principles are:

ul: Voluntary service - the salvor owes no pre-existing duty; a tug already under a towage contract is not salving.
Real danger to a vessel or other property in navigable waters.
"No cure, no pay" - by Article 12, only operations which have had a useful result give rise to payment.

A reward fixed to encourage salvage, on the ten criteria of Article 13(1) - salved value; skill and efforts in preventing environmental damage; measure of success; degree of danger; skill in salving vessel, property and life; time, expenses and losses; risk of liability; promptness; availability of salvage equipment; and its readiness, efficiency and value. The reward may not exceed the salved value.

Environmental protection in its own right - where the vessel or cargo threatened environmental damage, Article 14 gives the salvor special compensation (his expenses) even with no Article 13 reward, increasable by up to 30%, and by a tribunal to a maximum of 100% of expenses.

Duties both ways (Article 8) - the salvor to exercise due care, minimise environmental damage and accept other salvors when reasonably required; the owner and master to co-operate and accept redelivery when reasonably requested.

blocks.p: In practice salvage is contracted on Lloyd's Open Form; because Article 14 proved slow and contentious to assess, the industry added the SCOPIC clause in 2000 - an agreed tariff with a fixed uplift, which the salvor may invoke in place of Article 14.

General Average is the principle that where a sacrifice or extraordinary expenditure is made deliberately to save a common maritime adventure, the loss is shared by all the interests saved rather than left on the party that bore it. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules: there is a general average act "when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure". In Indian law a general average loss is defined at section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Every element must be present: a real common peril; an extraordinary act, not one the ship was already bound to do; intentional and voluntary; reasonable; for the common safety, not one interest alone; and property saved to contribute. The Rules are contractual, not statutory - they bind only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, which is why those documents name the edition.

The party who made the sacrifice or incurred the expenditure is entitled to contribution from every interest saved - ship, cargo and freight at risk - rateably on their contributory values at the time and place the adventure ends. It requires the Rule A elements and a loss that is a direct consequence of the act. It is defeated by the actionable fault of the claiming party: a shipowner whose unseaworthiness caused the casualty recovers nothing, because the Rules preserve the other parties' defences. Since cargo is released before the adjustment is finished, the owner exercises a lien on cargo and takes security first - an average bond with a general average guarantee from cargo underwriters, or a cash deposit.

"Artificial" general average describes allowances which the numbered Rules permit although they do not satisfy the strict common-safety test in Rule A. The clearest examples are port of refuge expenses and the wages and maintenance of crew during the detention there: once the ship has reached a place of safety the common safety is already secured, so that further expenditure is incurred for the common benefit of completing the adventure rather than to escape peril. The Rules allow it as a practical commercial compromise. The term is practitioner usage, not a defined category of the Rules, and the examinable point is the distinction it marks - general average in principle rests on common safety, while in practice the Rules also extend it to common benefit.

Adjustment turns the casualty into a settled apportionment, carried out by an average adjuster - appointed and paid by the shipowner but required to act impartially between all interests. The adjuster neither declares general average nor determines liability. The work is to collect security before cargo is released; decide which sacrifices and expenditures are allowable under the applicable edition; ascertain contributory values at the termination of the adventure; apportion rateably; and issue the general average statement. Large casualties take years, which is why the security taken at the outset matters.

The adjustment is not binding. It is a skilled statement of account and strong evidence, but any interest - most often cargo underwriters - may contest it. The usual grounds are that there was no general average act at all; that the expenditure was not extraordinary or not reasonable; that an allowance is not permitted by the incorporated edition; that contributory values or allowances are wrongly assessed; that the wrong edition has been applied; or, most powerfully, that the casualty was caused by the actionable fault of the claiming party, so that no contribution is due at all. It is resolved by negotiation, arbitration, or the courts of the jurisdiction the contract of carriage provides for.

The marks are printed, which is a gift: 4 + 4 + 8. Give salvage a quarter of the answer and no more, define General Average tightly, and then spend half the answer on the four named sub-items. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write a long general essay on general average and then deal with entitlement, artificial, adjustment and contestation in a sentence each. Each of those four is worth about two marks - give each of them its own heading so the examiner can see all four have been answered.

blocks.h: The four sub-items are a lifecycle - use that

blocks.p: They are not four unrelated definitions. Read in order they describe what happens after a casualty: who may claim (entitlement), what may be claimed even though strict principle would exclude it (artificial), how the claim is worked out (adjustment), and how it is fought (contestation). Presenting them as a sequence turns a list into an argument, and it makes them far easier to recall.

This is the item most candidates cannot place, and precision matters. Artificial general average is not fraud and not a fictitious claim. It is the name practitioners give to allowances the numbered Rules permit even though the common safety has already been achieved - classically port of refuge expenses and crew wages and maintenance during the detention. The underlying distinction is common safety (the Rule A test) against common benefit (completing the adventure). Say that distinction explicitly and the mark is earned. Be careful to present the term as accepted usage rather than as a defined category of the Rules, because it is not defined in them.

blocks.h: Salvage and General Average are different things

blocks.p: They meet - a salvage award is commonly allowed in general average and apportioned across the interests - but they are not the same. Salvage is a reward to a stranger for a voluntary service to property in danger, governed by a convention. General Average is a sharing of loss between parties already joined in one adventure, governed by contract. A candidate who blurs them will struggle with 'artificial', because the reason salvage and port of refuge expenses need special treatment is precisely that they sit at the join.

ul: Treating the York-Antwerp Rules as law. They are contractual and apply only because a bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them; the edition named in the contract governs.
Saying the average adjuster declares general average or decides liability. The shipowner, normally through the master, declares it; the adjuster apportions it.
Forgetting security. Without an average bond and a GA guarantee, the shipowner has released the cargo and lost the lien that protects the claim.
Omitting the actionable fault defence, which is the single most important limit on entitlement and the strongest ground of contestation.
Writing that a salvor is always paid. Article 12 is "no cure, no pay" - and the Article 14 environmental exception exists precisely because that rule was leaving environmental salvage unrewarded.
Quoting an Article 13 reward that exceeds the salved value. It cannot.

blocks.p:
"The salvor saved the environment but not the ship - what does he get?" Not an Article 13 reward, because there was no useful result in property terms. He may claim Article 14 special compensation - his expenses, increasable by up to 30% and by a tribunal up to 100% - or, if invoked, SCOPIC remuneration under the contract.

"Is the adjuster's statement final?" No. It is evidence, not a judgment, and it can be contested on the grounds above.

"Which edition of the Rules applies?" Whichever the contract of carriage incorporates. YAR 2016 was adopted by the CMI in May 2016 and BIMCO forms refer to it, but older contracts still commonly incorporate YAR 1994.

ul: State Rule A. "There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure."
Where is general average defined in Indian law? Section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Give two examples of artificial general average. Port of refuge expenses, and crew wages and maintenance during the detention there.
What security does the shipowner take before releasing cargo? An average bond from cargo interests and a general average guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit.
What is SCOPIC and why does it exist? A contractual tariff annexed to Lloyd's Open Form, introduced in 2000, because assessing Article 14 special compensation proved slow and contentious.
Can a shipowner claim contribution if his own unseaworthiness caused the casualty? No - actionable fault defeats the claim.

blocks.p: Salvage: V-D-U-R-E - Voluntary, Danger, Useful result (no cure no pay), Reward under the Article 13 criteria capped at salved value, Environment under Article 14 and SCOPIC. General Average: Rule A, then the four printed items as a lifecycle - who claims, what counts, who works it out, who fights it (steps 3 to 6).

Salvage Convention Article 12 - payment only where the operations had a useful result
Salvage Convention Article 13(1)(a) to (j) - the ten criteria for fixing the reward; Article 13(3) - reward not to exceed the salved value
Salvage Convention Article 14 - special compensation; increase up to 30%, and to a maximum of 100% of expenses at a tribunal's discretion
Lloyd's Open Form and the SCOPIC clause (2000) - contractual, with a tariff and a fixed uplift, invoked in place of Article 14

blocks.p: Two points of honesty. First, "artificial general average" is practitioner terminology, not a defined term of the York-Antwerp Rules. It is used consistently in the adjusting profession to describe allowances made on a common-benefit basis where the strict Rule A common-safety test is not met, and this answer explains it in those terms; a candidate should present it as accepted usage and explain the underlying common safety versus common benefit distinction, which is what the mark is really for. Second, which edition of the Rules applies is a matter of the contract, not of law, so no answer can assert that YAR 2016 governs a given casualty. The Salvage Convention figures - the useful-result rule, the ten Article 13 criteria, the salved-value ceiling and the 30% and 100% uplifts in Article 14 - have been read in the Convention text and are stated exactly. The SCOPIC description rests on authoritative industry material rather than on a convention, because SCOPIC is a contract clause and not a treaty.

questions.understand_first: Salvage and general average both answer the question "who pays when a ship gets into trouble", but they answer it about different people. Salvage is about paying an outsider who chose to come and help. General average is about splitting a deliberate loss between the people who were already in the adventure together. Once that split is clear, the four sub-items are simply the life of a general average claim: who may claim, what the Rules let them claim, how it is calculated, and how it is fought.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: Worth learning close to verbatim - the phrase "when, and only when" carries the whole test.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is "artificial" general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Practitioner term for allowances the numbered Rules permit although the strict Rule A common-safety test is not met - classically port of refuge expenses and crew wages and maintenance during detention. The basis is common BENEFIT rather than common safety.
retrieval_cards.why: Not defined in the Rules. The mark is for the common safety versus common benefit distinction.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the "no cure, no pay" rule and where is it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 12 of the Salvage Convention 1989: salvage operations which have had a useful result give rise to a reward; if there is no useful result, no payment is due.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does Article 14 special compensation provide?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the vessel or its cargo threatened damage to the environment and the salvor earned no adequate Article 13 reward, he recovers his expenses, increasable by up to 30%, and by a tribunal to a maximum of 100% of expenses where he prevented or minimised environmental damage.
retrieval_cards.why: The 30% and 100% figures are examinable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are the York-Antwerp Rules law?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. They are contractual and bind only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them - which is why the contract names the edition. Absent incorporation, general average falls back on the applicable national law.
retrieval_cards.why: A very common error, and it also explains why the edition question exists.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who declares general average, and who adjusts it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The shipowner, normally through the master, declares it. An independent average adjuster - appointed and paid by the owner but acting impartially between all interests - prepares the adjustment. The adjuster decides neither the declaration nor liability.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What single defence defeats an entitlement to contribution outright?
retrieval_cards.answer: Actionable fault. If the peril was caused by the claiming party's actionable fault - for example a shipowner's unseaworthiness - no contribution is recoverable, because the Rules preserve the other parties' defences.
retrieval_cards.why: It is both the main limit on entitlement and the strongest ground of contestation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What security is taken before cargo is released, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: An average bond from cargo interests and a general average guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit. Once cargo is released the shipowner loses the lien that protects the claim, and adjustments can take years.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the average adjuster's statement final?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is a skilled statement of account and strong evidence, but not a judgment. Any interest may contest it - on whether there was a GA act, reasonableness, allowances, values, the edition applied, or actionable fault.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what "contestation" is asking about.

blocks.h: 1. What the owner is exposed to

blocks.p: Identify the exposures before naming any cover: loss of the ship; loss of the cargo; oil pollution from persistent cargo oil and bunkers; salvage, already under way; wreck location, marking and removal; crew death or injury; and claims by the coastal state and third parties. She sank in the territorial sea, where by UNCLOS Article 2 the coastal state has full sovereignty - so its law and its convention obligations govern what may be demanded of the owner.

ul: H&M insures the owner's own property interest in the ship, on standard terms such as the Institute Time Clauses (Hulls), the International Hull Clauses or the Nordic Plan. Explosion is ordinarily an insured peril.

Because the vessel sank, the claim will be an actual total loss where the ship is irretrievably lost, or a constructive total loss where recovery and repair would exceed the insured value - in which case the owner serves a notice of abandonment.
Sue and labour expenses reasonably incurred to avert or minimise the loss are recoverable, which is significant here because salvage was in progress.
General average contributions and salvage charges falling on the ship are recoverable under the policy.

blocks.p: P&I is the mutual cover for third-party liabilities that H&M does not touch, and in this casualty it does most of the work: oil pollution, wreck removal where required by law, cargo liability, crew death, injury and repatriation, damage to fixed and floating objects, and certain fines. Clubs in the International Group share risk through a pooling and reinsurance structure, which is what makes a casualty of this size insurable. The club also issues the "blue cards" on which the state issues the ship's compulsory insurance certificates.

ul: CLC 1992 governs pollution damage from persistent oil carried in bulk as cargo. Liability is strict and is channelled to the registered owner; the owner may limit by tonnage unless the damage resulted from his personal act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result. It requires compulsory insurance and a certificate, and gives claimants a direct right of action against the insurer. It applies to pollution damage in the territory, territorial sea and EEZ of a State Party.

Fund Convention 1992 provides a second tier where CLC compensation is unavailable or insufficient, and the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003 a third tier for states that join it. Together these are the reason a tanker owner's exposure is finite while claimants remain compensated.

Bunkers Convention 2001 covers bunker pollution where CLC does not - principally non-tankers and tankers in ballast. It imposes strict liability on a broadly defined shipowner and requires compulsory insurance for ships over 1,000 GT. For a laden tanker such as this VLCC, CLC covers bunker-oil damage as well, so Bunkers is the fallback rather than the primary regime.

blocks.h: 5. Wreck removal, salvage and global limitation

ul: Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 (in force 14 April 2015) makes the registered owner strictly liable for locating, marking and removing a hazardous wreck, with compulsory insurance and a certificate for ships of 300 GT and above and a direct action against the insurer. It applies by default in the exclusive economic zone; it reaches the territorial sea only where the state has opted to extend it - so whether it governs here depends on that coastal state.

Salvage. The salvors' claim continues under the Salvage Convention 1989 - an Article 13 reward if there was a useful result, otherwise Article 14 special compensation, or SCOPIC remuneration if invoked under Lloyd's Open Form. The sinking does not extinguish the claim.

Global limitation. The LLMC 1976, as amended by the 1996 Protocol, allows the owner to constitute a limitation fund by tonnage for most maritime claims. Some states exclude wreck removal claims from limitation by reservation, and limitation is lost on the same conduct test as under CLC.

blocks.p: None of this is unconditional. Cover can be prejudiced by unseaworthiness or want of due diligence, breach of a class or trading warranty, non-disclosure - the contract is one of utmost good faith, governed in Indian law by sections 19 and 20 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 - and wilful misconduct. A tank explosion at once raises questions about inert gas operation, tank atmosphere control and the safety management system, and those answers decide both whether the policy responds and whether the owner keeps his right to limit. The immediate duties are practical: notify H&M and the club, preserve evidence, appoint surveyors, co-operate with the coastal and flag state investigations, and concede nothing on liability.

The question prints its own two limbs, (a) insurance and (b) conventions, so give them roughly eight marks each and keep them visibly separate. The strongest opening is the one used here - a short paragraph identifying the exposures before naming any cover. It shows you understand that insurance and conventions are two different answers to the same question: what happens to the money.

blocks.h: The two-axis idea that organises everything

blocks.p: There are two independent axes and candidates constantly collapse them. Axis one: whose loss. H&M covers the owner's own property; P&I covers his liability to others. Axis two: liability versus compensation. The conventions decide whether the owner is liable and how much he can limit; insurance decides who pays. CLC does not insure anybody - it imposes strict liability and then requires the owner to carry insurance for it. Say that sentence and you have the examiner's attention.

blocks.h: Why CLC and not Bunkers leads here

blocks.p: This is a VLCC and the casualty involved a tank explosion, so it was carrying persistent oil in bulk as cargo. That puts the casualty squarely inside CLC 1992, which then also covers the ship's bunker oil. The Bunkers Convention 2001 exists for the cases CLC leaves out - non-tankers, and tankers in ballast. Leading with Bunkers on a laden VLCC signals that the candidate has learned a list rather than a regime.

blocks.h: The territorial sea detail is deliberate

blocks.p: The examiner put the sinking in the territorial sea of a coastal state, not on the high seas, and that is worth marks. By UNCLOS Article 2 the coastal state has sovereignty there, so its law applies directly. It also creates the one genuine trap in the question: the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention applies automatically in the EEZ, and to the territorial sea only if the state has opted to extend it. Saying "Nairobi applies" flatly is an overstatement; saying it applies if that state has extended it is precise.

ul: Treating CLC as a form of insurance. It is a liability convention with a compulsory-insurance requirement attached.
Confusing the tiers. CLC is the owner, the 1992 Fund is the second tier, the Supplementary Fund is the third for states that join it.

Assuming the owner can always limit. Limitation is lost where the damage resulted from his personal act or omission with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.
Forgetting that the salvors still have a claim after the ship sinks - a useful result may be absent, but Article 14 or SCOPIC may not be.
Writing as though cover is automatic. Unseaworthiness, breach of warranty and non-disclosure are exactly the issues a tank explosion raises.
Ignoring the cargo interests entirely. The cargo owner has lost a VLCC parcel of oil and will be claiming.

blocks.p:
"The ship sank - is it a total loss?" Distinguish. An actual total loss is where the ship is destroyed or irretrievably deprived; a constructive total loss is where recovery and repair would cost more than the insured value, and it requires a notice of abandonment. The bare fact of sinking does not decide which.

"Who pays for removing the wreck?" The registered owner, strictly, under the Nairobi Convention where it applies - and his P&I club in practice, subject to the certificate and direct action.

"Does the salvage claim die with the ship?" No. Article 13 needs a useful result, but Article 14 special compensation and SCOPIC exist precisely for the case where the property is lost but the environment was protected.

ul: Difference between H&M and P&I? H&M is your own hull; P&I is your liability to third parties, on a mutual basis.
On whom does CLC channel liability? The registered owner, strictly, with a right to limit by tonnage and compulsory insurance behind it.
When did the Nairobi Convention enter into force, and where does it apply? 14 April 2015; in the EEZ by default and in the territorial sea only where the state extends it.
What is a blue card? The club's confirmation of cover, on the strength of which a state issues the ship's compulsory insurance certificate under CLC or Bunkers.
What breaks the right to limit? The owner's personal act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result.
What would you do in the first hour as Chief Engineer? Preserve records and data, secure the evidence, report through the master to owners, club and flag state, and give nothing away on liability.

blocks.p: OWN - OTHERS - OIL - WRECK - LIMIT. Own property is H&M and total loss (step 2). Others is P&I (step 3). Oil is CLC, Fund and Supplementary Fund, with Bunkers as the fallback (step 4). Wreck brings in Nairobi and the continuing salvage claim (step 5). Limit is LLMC, and the conduct that destroys it (steps 5 and 6).

The answer therefore treats causation as the open question rather than assuming a covered peril.

The often-quoted rule that corrosion rate roughly doubles for each 10 degrees Celsius rise is a general kinetic approximation, not a coating or class standard. It is stated as an approximation and qualified by the oxygen-solubility effect.

blocks.h: 1. Why tank coatings are a statutory matter

blocks.p: Corrosion is the principal structural degradation mechanism in ballast and cargo tanks, and the response is regulated rather than left to maintenance policy. SOLAS regulation II-1/3-2 requires protective coatings for dedicated seawater ballast tanks in all ship types and for double-side skin spaces of bulk carriers, complying with the Performance Standard for Protective Coatings, IMO resolution MSC.215(82). The PSPC is written to a target useful coating life of 15 years, which section 4.1 defines as the period over which the system is intended to remain in "GOOD" condition. The coating, not the steel, is therefore the thing being managed.

blocks.h: 2. Influence of temperature on corrosion rate

ul: Corrosion in a tank is an electrochemical process, and its rate rises with temperature - as a rough kinetic approximation the rate roughly doubles for each 10°C rise over the normal range.

That is offset by a competing effect: the solubility of dissolved oxygen falls as temperature rises. In a vented tank where oxygen can escape, the rate therefore peaks and then falls at higher temperatures; in a closed or continuously replenished system it keeps climbing.

Heated boundaries dominate in practice. Ballast tanks adjacent to heated cargo tanks, heated fuel tanks or the machinery space run warmer than the sea and corrode faster than identical tanks elsewhere in the ship.

Temperature cycling is worse than steady heat. It drives condensation on the underdeck and upper structure, so those surfaces undergo repeated wet and dry cycling - the most aggressive condition, because the surface is continually re-oxygenated.

In cargo oil tanks the effect is chemical too: heated crude raises the temperature while inert gas contributes carbon dioxide and sulphur oxides, which dissolve in the condensate to form acids - hence severe underdeck corrosion and pitting on the tank bottom beneath water and sludge.
Defective surface preparation - mill scale left in place, residual soluble salts, inadequate blast profile or cleanliness. This is the single largest cause, and it is built in at construction.
Application faults - dry film thickness below specification, missed stripe coats at edges and welds, dry spray, and application outside the coating's temperature, humidity or dew-point limits.
Edges, welds and cut-outs - sharp edges and weld spatter hold too little paint, so breakdown starts there and spreads.
Mechanical damage from ballasting and cargo operations, staging, tools, hose handling and crew traffic.
Ageing and chemical attack - chalking, embrittlement, loss of adhesion, osmotic blistering, cathodic disbondment, and attack by heated or chemical cargoes and by tank cleaning.
Design and access - poor drainage, pockets that never dry, and areas that cannot be reached for inspection or repair.
Deferred maintenance. Breakdown is self-accelerating: once rust creeps under the film, adjacent coating is undermined.

blocks.h: 4. How coating condition assessment reveals corrosion status

blocks.p: Coating condition is assessed visually and reported in three grades used throughout the survey regime: GOOD - only minor spot rusting; FAIR - local breakdown at edges of stiffeners and weld connections, and/or light rusting over 20% or more of the areas under consideration, but less than POOR; and POOR - general breakdown of coating over 20% or more of the areas, or hard scale over 10% or more of the areas under consideration.

ul: It is a leading indicator. Coating breakdown shows where corrosion will occur before any measurable steel is lost, whereas thickness measurement is a lagging indicator that reports damage already done.

It drives the survey regime. Under the Enhanced Survey Programme a rating below GOOD must be recorded and re-examined at subsequent annual surveys, and a POOR rating brings extended examination and thickness measurement.
It targets effort - telling the Chief Engineer and the surveyor which tanks and which specific areas need close-up survey, re-coating or steel renewal.
It is judged alongside anode condition, so coating and cathodic protection are assessed as one system.

blocks.h: 5. Information obtained from the Coating Technical File

blocks.p: The CTF is required by PSPC section 3.4, is reviewed by the Administration, and by section 3.4.5 must be kept on board and maintained throughout the life of the ship. It carries the specification of the coating system, the record of the shipyard's and owner's coating work, and the criteria for coating selection, job specification, inspection, maintenance and repair. At new construction (section 3.4.2) it must contain:

ul: the Statement of Compliance or Type Approval Certificate for the coating system;

the Technical Data Sheet - product name and identification, materials, components, composition and colours, minimum and maximum dry film thickness, application methods and tools, the required condition of the surface to be coated (de-rusting grade, cleanliness and profile), and environmental limitations of temperature and humidity;

shipyard work records - the actual space and area coated in square metres, the coating system applied, time of coating, thickness and number of layers, ambient conditions during coating, and the method of surface preparation;
procedures for inspection and repair of the coating during construction;
the coating log issued by the coating inspector, confirming application in accordance with the specification and recording any deviations, with the daily log and non-conformity reports;
the shipyard's verified inspection report - completion date, result, remarks and inspector's signature; and
procedures for in-service maintenance and repair of the coating system.

blocks.p: Thereafter in-service maintenance, repair and partial re-coating are recorded in it (3.4.3), and a full re-coating requires the 3.4.2 items again (3.4.4). The file is the ship's coating history: what was specified, what was actually applied and under what conditions, and everything done since.

Four printed sub-items, no printed marks, so treat them as four equal quarters and give each its own heading. The verbs differ and you should follow them: discuss for the first two, describe for the third, and state for the fourth. Sub-item (iv) is a list question - the marks are in naming the CTF contents, not in writing an essay about coatings, so give it as a list and make it complete.

blocks.h: The temperature answer needs both effects

blocks.p: Most candidates write only "hotter means faster" and stop. The complete answer has two competing effects: reaction kinetics rise with temperature, but dissolved oxygen solubility falls. In a vented tank where oxygen escapes the rate peaks and then declines; in a closed system it keeps rising. Then add the point that actually matters on a ship - cycling beats steady heat, because wet and dry cycling on the underdeck continually re-oxygenates the surface. Say that the corrosion rate roughly doubles per 10°C as an approximation, not as a standard; it is general kinetics, not a class rule.

blocks.h: Coating condition is a leading indicator - this is the point of (iii)

blocks.p: Sub-item (iii) asks how coating assessment makes you aware of the corrosion status, and the answer is about timing. Coating breakdown tells you where corrosion is going to happen; thickness measurement tells you where it already has. That is why the survey regime is keyed to the coating grade rather than to steel loss - by the time the steel is measurably thin, the opportunity to intervene cheaply has gone. If you write one sentence in this sub-item, write that one.

ul: Answering (iv) with generalities about coatings. It says state the information obtained - it wants the CTF's actual contents.
Confusing the Coating Technical File with the Ship Construction File or the Survey Report File. The CTF is coatings only, required by the PSPC, kept on board for the life of the ship.
Giving the 10°C doubling rule as though it were a regulatory figure, and omitting the oxygen-solubility counter-effect.

Quoting the GOOD / FAIR / POOR percentages loosely. FAIR is light rusting over 20% or more but less than POOR; POOR is general breakdown over 20% or more, or hard scale over 10% or more. The hard-scale limb is the one people forget.
Treating coating breakdown as a painting problem. It is a survey-driver: the grade changes what class requires of the ship.

blocks.p:
"What is the target useful life of a PSPC coating?" Fifteen years - but say what that means. Section 4.1 defines it as the period over which the system is intended to remain in GOOD condition, and it adds that actual life varies with conditions in service. It is a design target, not a guarantee or a replacement interval.

"Where does GOOD condition come from?" PSPC section 2.6 defines it as the condition with minor spot rusting, referring across to the ESP regime - so the coating standard and the survey standard use the same vocabulary deliberately.

"Which tanks does the PSPC cover?" Dedicated seawater ballast tanks in all ship types and double-side skin spaces of bulk carriers. Cargo oil tanks of crude oil tankers are covered by a separate, later performance standard - do not merge them.

ul: What is the 90/10 rule? PSPC section 2.8 - 90% of all thickness measurements shall be at or above the nominal dry film thickness, and none of the remaining 10% below 0.9 times NDFT.
What is a stripe coat and why does it matter? Extra painting of edges, welds and hard-to-reach areas, because those are where film thickness is naturally lowest and breakdown begins.
How long is the CTF kept? On board and maintained throughout the life of the ship - PSPC section 3.4.5.
What happens if a ballast tank is rated POOR? It is recorded, re-examined at subsequent annual surveys and brings extended examination and thickness measurement.
Why do ballast tanks next to heated cargo corrode faster? Higher steel temperature raises the electrochemical rate, and the temperature difference promotes condensation and wet-dry cycling.
What is recorded in the CTF after a partial re-coat? The maintenance, repair and partial re-coating activities, under section 3.4.3; a full re-coating requires the 3.4.2 items again.

blocks.p: The four sub-items are a life cycle of the coating: WHY IT CORRODES (temperature), WHY THE PAINT FAILS (deterioration), HOW YOU KNOW (condition assessment), WHERE IT IS WRITTEN DOWN (the CTF). For the CTF contents themselves, work in build order: certificate, data sheet, what the yard actually did, how it was inspected, how it is repaired - that ordering reproduces PSPC 3.4.2 almost item for item.

questions.understand_first: The regulation does not try to stop steel corroding. It manages the barrier between the steel and the water, and then builds the whole survey system on the condition of that barrier. Once you see that the coating is the regulated object - specified to a fifteen-year target, documented in its own file, and graded at every survey - the four sub-items stop being separate topics and become one story: what attacks the coating, why it fails, how its condition is judged, and where its history is written down.

blocks.p: Ship health and vector control are governed by the International Health Regulations (2005), a binding instrument of the World Health Organization, as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024. The 2024 amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025. The IHR work through designated points of entry, competent authorities at those points, and a small set of ship documents.

ul: It makes the rules. WHO adopts the IHR and prescribes the model certificates in Annex 3 and the Ship Declaration of Health in Annex 8, so the documents are the same worldwide.

It identifies where vector control is needed. Under Annex 5, WHO publishes on a regular basis a list of areas where disinsection or other vector control measures are recommended for conveyances arriving from them, through temporary or standing recommendations.

It advises methods and materials. Where WHO has advised methods for disinsection, deratting, disinfection or decontamination, those should be used unless the competent authority is satisfied that others are as safe and reliable (Article 27), and States should accept measures applied elsewhere by WHO-advised methods.

It certifies and publishes. On a State Party's request WHO may, after appropriate investigation, certify that a port meets the IHR requirements (Article 20(4)), publishes certification guidelines and the list of certified ports (20(5)), and publishes the lists of authorized ports notified by States Parties (20(3)).

It provides technical guidance - notably the WHO Handbook for inspection of ships and issuance of ship sanitation certificates - and declares Public Health Emergencies of International Concern with temporary recommendations.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - the health authority for IHR purposes, under which the National IHR Focal Point sits.

Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), and under it the Port Health Organisation, headed by the Port Health Officer - the competent authority at the point of entry. It inspects ships, baggage, cargo and containers, supervises control measures and issues the ship sanitation certificates, working under the Indian Port Health Rules, 1955 with the IHR 2005.
Directorate General of Shipping, through its Maritime Health Branch, on the seafarer side - approving medical examiners and governing seafarers' medical fitness examination and certification.
Port authorities and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways support these functions at the ports themselves.

Ship Sanitation Control Exemption Certificate (SSCEC) - issued where the competent authority is satisfied that the ship is free of infection and contamination, including vectors and reservoirs, so that no control measures are required (Article 39(6)).

Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (SSCC) - issued where control measures were required and have been satisfactorily completed, and it records the evidence found and the measures taken (Article 39(5)). Under Annex 5 the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them are recorded on this certificate. If a satisfactory result could not be obtained, the authority notes that on the certificate (Article 39(7)).

blocks.p: Both follow the model in Annex 3, and they replaced the former Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates. Alongside them the master submits a Ship Declaration of Health under Article 37, to the model in Annex 8 - a declaration, not a certificate. Separately, and concerning the crew rather than the ship, seafarers hold medical fitness certificates under MLC 2006 and STCW.

blocks.h: 5. Issue in India, validity and extension

ul: In India they are issued by the Port Health Officer at a port authorized for the purpose and notified to WHO. Under Article 20(3) a State Party notifies which ports may issue the SSCC, which may issue the SSCEC only, and which may grant the one-month extension.
Validity: a maximum of six months, for both the SSCEC and the SSCC (Article 39(1)).
Extension: by one month, where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at that port - the extension carries the ship to a port where the certificate can be obtained.

Where no valid certificate is produced, or evidence of a public health risk is found on board, the State Party may proceed under Article 27(1) - treating the ship as affected and requiring disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Control measures are to be carried out whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading (Article 39(4)).

For Indian coastal trade calling where no Port Health Officer is available, DG Shipping has provided for a Statement of Compliance issued by an authorized medical examiner, to be endorsed at the earliest available opportunity.

blocks.p: Four separate questions are asked and each must be visibly answered - WHO's role, the national agencies, the certificates, and issue/validity/extension in India. Take them in the printed order and head each one. The final limb contains the two numbers the examiner is certainly looking for, six months and one month, so never let it be squeezed by a long essay on WHO.

blocks.h: The currency point that will separate answers

blocks.p: The IHR were amended in 2024 and those amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025 - before this paper was sat. One visible consequence: Article 37 is now the "Ship Declaration of Health". In the original 2005 text it was the "Maritime Declaration of Health", and that older name is what almost every textbook, coaching note and older syllabus still uses. Both texts were compared directly for this answer: the original uses "Maritime Declaration of Health" throughout and never the new name; the consolidated amended text uses "Ship Declaration of Health" throughout and never the old one. Using the current name, and being able to say why it changed, is a cheap and genuine mark.

blocks.h: Ship health and crew health are two different systems

blocks.p: The question asks about "the ship and the crew", and the two run on separate tracks with separate authorities. Ship health is WHO and the IHR, administered in India by the Port Health Organisation under DGHS and the Ministry of Health, and evidenced by the SSCC or SSCEC. Crew health is MLC 2006 and STCW, administered in India by DG Shipping through approved medical examiners, and evidenced by seafarers' medical fitness certificates. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates. It is not - the Port Health Officer issues those.

ul: Calling the SSCC/SSCEC a Deratting Certificate. Those were the predecessors under the earlier Regulations and were replaced under the IHR 2005 - the scope widened from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.
Saying the certificates are valid for six months extendable by six months. The extension is one month, and only where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at that port.
Confusing the SSCC with the SSCEC. Exemption means no measures were needed; Control means measures were required and were completed.
Treating the Ship Declaration of Health as a certificate. It is a declaration by the master, to the Annex 8 model, and a State may dispense with it entirely under Article 37(4).
Naming WHO as an enforcement body. WHO recommends, certifies ports on request and publishes; the competent authority at the point of entry enforces.

blocks.p:
"Your certificate expired yesterday and the port cannot inspect - what happens?" The one-month extension in Article 39(1) exists precisely for this, and under Article 20(3)(c) States notify which of their ports may grant it, so that the ship can reach a port where the certificate is obtainable.

"When should the inspection be done?" Whenever possible with the ship and holds empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading - Article 39(4). Answering "any time" misses a printed requirement.

"What does WHO actually do about mosquitoes?" It publishes the list of areas where vector control is recommended for conveyances arriving from them, and advises the methods. States Parties then run vector control programmes at points of entry - to a minimum distance of 400 metres from the operational areas under Annex 5.

ul: Who issues the SSCC in India? The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO.
Under which ministry does the Port Health Organisation sit? The Directorate General of Health Services, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Validity and extension? Maximum six months; extendable by one month where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at the port.
What is recorded on an SSCC? The evidence found and the control measures taken - including, under Annex 5, the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them.
What happens if you cannot produce a valid certificate? The State Party may treat the ship as affected under Article 27(1) and require disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Which convention covers the crew's medical fitness rather than the ship's sanitation? MLC 2006, with STCW for certification - administered in India by DG Shipping.

blocks.p: RULE - AGENCY - PAPER - CLOCK. Rule: IHR 2005 as amended, WHO's role (steps 1 to 2). Agency: MoHFW, DGHS, Port Health Organisation and the Port Health Officer, with DG Shipping on the crew side (step 3). Paper: SSCEC, SSCC, and the Ship Declaration of Health (step 4). Clock: six months, plus one (step 5). Two numbers, two certificates, one declaration.

questions.understand_first: There are two health systems on a ship and the question runs across both. One protects the world from the ship - vectors, infection and contamination crossing borders in a hull - and that is WHO's International Health Regulations, enforced by a port health authority and evidenced by a ship sanitation certificate. The other protects the crew, and that is labour and training law administered by the shipping administration. Keeping those two apart is what makes the India limb straightforward: the Port Health Officer certifies the ship, DG Shipping certifies the seafarer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the SSCC from the SSCEC.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Exemption Certificate is issued where the authority is satisfied the ship is free of infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs, so no measures are needed. The Control Certificate is issued where measures were required and satisfactorily completed, and records the evidence found and the measures taken.
retrieval_cards.why: Exemption means nothing was needed; Control means something was done.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is Article 37 called now, and what was it called before?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Ship Declaration of Health, to the model in Annex 8. In the original 2005 text it was the Maritime Declaration of Health. The change came with the amendments in force from 19 September 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: Most textbooks and coaching notes still use the old name.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are these still called Deratting Certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates of the earlier Regulations were replaced under the IHR 2005 by the SSCC and SSCEC, widening the scope from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.

The Port Health Organisation sits under the Directorate General of Health Services, within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and works under the Indian Port Health Rules 1955 with the IHR 2005.
retrieval_cards.why: Not DG Shipping - that side handles seafarer medical fitness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Summarise WHO's role in four verbs.
retrieval_cards.answer: It prescribes (the Regulations and the Annex 3 and 8 models), publishes (areas where vector control is recommended, and lists of authorized ports), advises (methods and materials for disinsection and deratting) and certifies (ports, on the State Party's request, under Article 20(4)).
retrieval_cards.why: WHO does not enforce - the competent authority at the point of entry does.
